summary: Describes how to identify the authoritative server for RDAP queries that are not for domains, addresses or AS numbers, such as entity queries. It is a Best Current Practice.

plainLanguage.summary: RDAP is the protocol a client uses to ask for registration data such as domain names, IP address allocations and the records of organisations and people. For most queries the client can work out which server is authoritative. For queries about organisations and people it cannot, because those identifiers have no built-in structure. This RFC adds a short tag to those identifiers so that the client can find the right server.

questions: how does an rdap client find the authoritative server for an entity
what is a service provider tag in rdap
subtitle: A hyphen and a short provider tag on the end of an RDAP handle tell clients which server to ask.

tldr.problem: RDAP can find the authoritative server for domain name, IP address and AS number queries, but not for entity queries, because entity handles have no structure that points to a provider.
tldr.mechanism: Providers append a tag made of a hyphen and an IANA-registered provider identifier to each handle, such as XXXX-ARIN. A client splits off the part after the last hyphen and looks it up in an IANA bootstrap registry to get the base RDAP URL.
tldr.outcome: Entity queries, and other unstructured identifiers, can now be bootstrapped to the right server. Responses that use the practice must say so with the rdapConformance value rdap_objectTag_level_0.

today: RFC 8521 is a Best Current Practice and, per the metadata, has not been obsoleted or updated by a later RFC. It updates RFC 7484.

sections.title: Introduction
sections.content:
The Registration Data Access Protocol (RDAP) includes a method, described in RFC 7484, for identifying the authoritative server that handles domain name, IP address and Autonomous System Number (ASN) queries. The method works because each of those data elements is structured in a way that helps a client parse it and associate it with a particular RDAP service provider. Domain names, for example, include labels such as com, net and org that are associated with specific service providers.

As noted in Section 9 of RFC 7484, the method does not describe how to identify the authoritative server for entity queries, name server queries, help queries, or queries using certain search patterns. The reason is that the identifiers bound to those queries are not structured in a way that makes it easy to associate an identifier with a particular service provider.

This document describes an operational practice that adds structure to RDAP identifiers, so that the authoritative server can be identified for those additional queries as well.
sections.plainLanguage: When a client asks RDAP for a domain name or an address, the identifier itself says which registry holds the answer. When it asks about an organisation or a person, the identifier says nothing, so the client has no way to find the right server. This RFC gives those identifiers a small, structured ending so the client can find the server.

sections.title: The Object Naming Practice
sections.content:
A service provider tag is constructed by prepending the Unicode HYPHEN-MINUS character, U+002D, which RFC 3986 describes as an unreserved character, to an IANA-registered value that represents the service provider. The tag for a service provider identified by the string value ARIN is written as -ARIN.

Together with the rdapConformance attribute described in Section 4, service provider tags are concatenated to the end of RDAP query object identifiers, so that the authoritative server for a query can be identified without doubt. An RDAP entity handle can then be built so that a client can bootstrap an entity query. The identifier XXXX-ARIN finds the information for the entity with handle XXXX at service provider ARIN.

A client parses this identifier into a handle and a service provider identifier. Handles can themselves contain hyphen characters, so the service provider identifier is whatever follows the last hyphen in the tagged identifier. The service provider identifier is used to retrieve a base RDAP URL from an IANA registry, and the base URL and the entity handle are then used to form a complete query path segment. If the base RDAP URL https://example.com/rdap/ is associated with service provider YYYY in an IANA registry, a client parses the tagged identifier XXXX-YYYY into the handle XXXX and the service provider YYYY, looks up the base URL, and forms the complete query URL https://example.com/rdap/entity/XXXX-YYYY.
sections.plainLanguage: The tag is a hyphen followed by a short code for the provider, for example -ARIN, and it goes at the end of the identifier. A client splits the identifier at its last hyphen, so the part before it is the handle and the part after it is the provider code. The provider code leads to a base address for the RDAP service, and the client adds the handle to build the final query address.

sections.title: Tagged Handles in RDAP Responses
sections.content:
Putting the practice into use requires tagging the unstructured identifiers that appear in RDAP responses, because those are the identifiers a client may use in a later query. The RFC gives two examples of responses with tagged handles. In the first, the domain, the entity and the network all carry the handle XXXX-RIR, and the network names the parent handle YYYY-RIR. In the second, the domain handle is XXXX-YYY-DNR, the two name server handles are XXXX-DNR, and the entity handle is XXXX-ABC.

RDAP responses can contain self links, which point back at the object being returned. Service provider tags and self references should be consistent with each other. When they are not, the service provider tag is processed with higher priority when the values are used to identify a service provider.
sections.plainLanguage: The identifiers that come back in a response have to carry the tag too, because that is what a client will quote in its next query. A response may also contain a link back to itself, and that link and the tag should agree; when they do not, the tag wins.

sections.title: The Risk of Hyphens and the Choice of Separator
sections.content:
There is a risk of unpredictable processing if the hyphen character is used for a natural, non-separator purpose inside an entity handle. A client could mistake such a hyphen for the separator and take the text that follows it to be a service provider identifier. A client that then queries the IANA registry for what it assumes is a valid service provider will likely get an unexpected, invalid result. For that reason, the use of the hyphen as a service provider tag separator must be noted by adding an rdapConformance value to query responses.

The hyphen was chosen as the separator for two reasons: it is a familiar separator character in operational use, and it avoids collision with URI-reserved characters. Section 2.3 of RFC 3986 lists several unreserved characters, namely ALPHA, DIGIT, hyphen, period, underscore and tilde. Letters and digits were excluded because they are commonly used in entity handles for non-separator purposes. The remaining characters were excluded because they are not broadly used as separators in entity handles.
sections.plainLanguage: Hyphens already appear inside many handles, so a client could misread part of a handle as a provider code. That is why the tag has to be declared in the response. The hyphen was picked because people already use it as a separator, and because it is one of the few characters that is safe in a web address.

sections.title: The Bootstrap Service Registry
sections.content:
The bootstrap service registry for the RDAP service provider space uses the structure specified in Section 3 of RFC 7484. Its JSON output holds contact information for the registered service provider identifiers, the alphanumeric identifiers themselves, and the base RDAP service URLs. Each entry lists a contact email address, the alphanumeric value that identifies the provider, and one or more URLs that provide the RDAP service for that registration. The URLs are expected to supply the same data, but they can differ in scheme or in other components as the service operator requires.

Service provider identifiers are alphanumeric and conform to the suffix portion, \w{1,8}, of the roidType syntax specified in Section 4.2 of RFC 5730.

The registry is populated under the First Come First Served policy of RFC 8126. Provider identifier values can be derived and assigned by IANA on request. A registration request includes an email address to associate with the registered identifier, the requested provider identifier, or an indication that IANA should assign one, and one or more base RDAP URLs to associate with it.
sections.plainLanguage: IANA keeps a registry that maps each provider code to the addresses of its RDAP service. A provider asks to be registered, giving a contact address, the code it wants, and its service addresses. Codes are handed out first come, first served, and follow a short alphanumeric format.

sections.title: RDAP Conformance
sections.content:
RDAP responses that contain values described in this document must indicate conformance with this specification by including the rdapConformance value rdap_objectTag_level_0. The example given in the RFC is a list of conformance values that holds the base value and the new one:

"rdapConformance" :
[
  "rdap_level_0",
  "rdap_objectTag_level_0"
]
sections.plainLanguage: A server that uses tagged identifiers says so in every response, by listing the value rdap_objectTag_level_0 among its conformance values. A client can then tell that the identifiers in that response carry a provider tag.

sections.title: IANA Considerations
sections.content:
IANA has created the RDAP Bootstrap Service Registry for Provider Object Tags and made it available as a JSON object. The formal syntax is the one specified in Section 10 of RFC 7484. Each entry holds an email address for the contact associated with the registered value, the alphanumeric value identifying the RDAP service provider, and one or more URLs that provide the RDAP service for that registration.

IANA has also registered an extension in the RDAP Extensions registry: the extension identifier is rdap_objectTag, the registry operator is Any, the published specification is this document, and the contact is the IESG. Its intended usage is to describe a best practice for structuring entity identifiers so that queries can be bootstrapped.
sections.plainLanguage: IANA keeps two things for this practice: the JSON registry of provider codes and service addresses, and a registry entry recording that the rdap_objectTag extension describes the best practice.

sections.title: Security Considerations
sections.content:
The practice uses IANA as a well-known, centrally trusted authority, so that users get RDAP data from an authoritative source. That reduces the risk of sending queries to non-authoritative sources and of divulging query information to unintended parties.

Using TLS 1.2 or TLS 1.3, which obsoletes TLS 1.2, to protect the connection to IANA lets the server authenticate itself as being operated by IANA and gives integrity protection for the referral information it returns, as well as privacy protection through data confidentiality. The RDAP connection that follows is performed as usual and keeps the security properties of the RDAP protocols themselves, described in RFC 7481.
sections.plainLanguage: Because the client reaches the right server through a registry run by IANA, it does not disclose its query to a random server. The connection to IANA must be protected with TLS, so that the client can check that it really is talking to IANA and that the referral has not been altered.

messages.label: Look up the provider code
messages.note: The client takes the text after the last hyphen and looks it up in the bootstrap registry.

messages.label: Base RDAP URL
messages.note: The registry returns the service addresses registered for that provider code.

messages.label: RDAP query
messages.note: The client builds the query path from the base URL and the handle, and asks the authoritative server.

viz.caption: The rules a client has to follow

items.title: Tag format
items.text: A hyphen followed by the IANA-registered value for the provider.

items.title: Split at the last hyphen
items.text: Handles may contain hyphens, so the provider code is whatever follows the last one.

items.title: Declare the tag
items.text: A response using tagged identifiers lists rdap_objectTag_level_0 among its conformance values.

items.title: Registry lookup
items.text: The provider code is looked up in the IANA bootstrap registry to get the base RDAP URL.
